provenance.post_check: reviewer-name tokens replaced by [name] after the quote check

issues.text: The presentation of results is hard to follow: with many outcome variables and three treatment arms, the evaluator found it difficult to tell which results belong to which arm, which the evaluator sees as the main quibble with the study.
issues.quote:
I found it difficult to follow which results belonged to which
arm. It was difficult to keep them all straight.

issues.text: The paper lacks a summary table comparing effect sizes across arms and outcomes, including tests of whether effect sizes differ between arms; the evaluator suggests grouping outcomes by type and possibly color-coding relative effect size.
issues.quote:
I would have much
appreciated a summary table comparing the size of results (and also
noting if it was possible to reject the hypothesis that the effect sizes
were the same).

issues.text: The paper raises but does not answer the policy-relevant question of whether recipients' income and asset gains are at least as large as the transfer amount; the evaluator notes this comparison is only derivable from the results and is not presented.
issues.quote:
While
it is possible to calculate if this is true from the results in the
paper (e.g. from income and asset changes), this summary is not
presented in the paper.

issues.text: The general equilibrium price result is imprecise: the authors fail to reject the null of no village-level price inflation, so the evidence does not establish a precise zero.
issues.quote:
they note
that they are simply not rejecting the null; this is not a precise
zero.

issues.text: The interpretation that recipients are severely credit-constrained and that the UBI does not relieve this is the evaluator's inference, and it rests on the surprising similarity of lump-sum and long-term UBI effects rather than direct evidence on credit constraints.
issues.quote:
This, to [me], suggests that recipients are extremely
credit-constrained - and that this is not alleviated by the UBI.

issues.text: The claim that the UBI would not reduce work is questioned for transfers large enough to cover all basic needs, since the study's transfer size may not generalise to such cases.
issues.quote:
though it is not clear to me
that this would be true in a case where the UBI was large enough to
cover all basic needs
